newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Credit Lyonnais recovery may have lost it fresh cash.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Credit Lyonnais recovery may have lost it fresh cash.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais' unexpectedly robust recovery from its reckless expansion may be behind the French government's surprise refusal to recapitalise the state-controlled bank, banking analysts say.

Along with the government's desire to limit the already huge cost to taxpayers of the bank's lending spree, Credit Lyonnais' financial revival could make a capital injection unacceptable to taxpayers and to rival institutions, analysts say.
"It would be a little shocking," one Paris analyst said. "There are elections coming up next year. Also, its competitors could complain it was hurting competition."

The government has already bailed out Credit Lyonnais twice since the bank nearly collapsed in the early 1990s under the weight of its lending excesses. It had been expected to inject at least 10 billion francs ($1.8 billion) more into Credit Lyonnais as part of a restructuring plan to ready it for privatisation.
But Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Sunday there was "no question of the state taking part in a new recapitalisation". The bank has declined to comment.

Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade has argued in the past that the bank needed new funds if it hoped to find a buyer because its capital adequacy ratios -- while above minimum solvency standards -- would be too low to attract investors.

But analysts say the bank may have undermined its arguments by its strong 1996 performance. Credit Lyonnais, which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, posted a 1996 net profit of 200 million francs, up from 13 milion a year earlier, and reported a 42 percent jump in operating profit.
For 1997, it pledged net profit in "the billions" of francs. "It's had a very strong recovery in operating terms. Those were good quality results," said Patrick Leguil of Transbourse.
GOOD RESULTS MAKE CAPITAL INJECTION LESS IMMEDIATELY NECESSARY
Analysts argue, even with a Tier One ratio of 4.6, which is below the French average of 6.0, the bank could find a buyer.
"Given the good set of results, it makes a capital injection much less immediately necessary -- and there are banks operating with solvency ratios of around 4.5," said one analyst.

Crucial, however, is what disposals could be demanded of the bank by the European Commission, which must approve the French government's restructuring plans and can veto state aid to ensure fair competition in the European Union.
Even without a recapitalisation, the Commission estimates the new plan will include 15 to 20 billion francs in government aid for softening terms of a 1995 state rescue package.

"The big unknown is what will be Credit Lyonnais' capital needs after the disposals. If the asset sales produce net losses, Credit Lyonnais could be in danger of falling below minimum regulatory solvency requirements," said an analyst.
The government had promised to submit the plan in February to the Commission. But government officials now say it will not be forwarded to the Commission until later this month.

"The issue right now is to find a balance that is fair to the shareholder (the state) and to the bank," a government source said. The source said Brussels was being kept informed and there was "no problem from that end".
Peyrelevade has said that the bank cannot endanger its future by selling off strategic operations and has hinted he might quit if its viability were jeopardised.

The bank is expected to sell most of its European retail network outside France to focus on wholesale banking and capital markets activities outside of its domestic market. But many of those assets were acquired at the market's peak.

The bank has ruled out selling for now its 50 percent stake in Germany's BfG Bank AG, a sale which bank officials say could trigger a five billion franc loss, as BfG's book value is considerably higher than its current market value.

Some analysts suggest that Brussels might accept a more gradual disposal of assets that would allow the bank to sell them when the market improved in exchange for the government's commitment to privatisation and minimum state aid.

Some analysts also said Arthuis' harder stance on recapitalisation might mean he wanted to accelerate the bank's sale. But government officials said Arthuis was still looking at late 1998 or early 1999 for the privatisation.
Analysts say they believe the bank is most likely be sold privately as there was too much public scepticism surrounding it to make a public share offering successful.
One analyst speculated that German insurer Allianz AG Holding, whose products are already sold over Credit Lyonnais counters, might buy into the bank in tandem with Deutsche Bank AG.

Estimates of the final bill for bailing out Credit Lyonnais, known as "Crazy Lyonnais" during its frantic expansion, range up to 130 million francs -- and higher. But Arthuis has said it is impossible at this stage to say what the tally will be.
($ = 5.668 French Francs)
